cards.front: What is the temporal dead zone?
cards.back: The span from the start of a scope until a `let`/`const`/`class` declaration runs. The binding exists but any read, even `typeof`, throws ReferenceError.

cards.front: Block scope vs function scope: which keywords use which?
cards.back: `let`/`const` are block-scoped (nearest `{ }`); `var` is function-scoped and hoisted as `undefined`.

cards.front: Why does `for (var i...) fns.push(() => i)` give all 3s, and how does `let` fix it?
cards.back: `var` gives one shared `i`, read after the loop ends (3). `let` in a for header makes a fresh binding per iteration, so each closure keeps its own value.

cards.front: Does a closure capture a variable's value or the variable?
cards.back: The variable. It sees later reassignments, and each factory call creates a new, private environment.

cards.front: How does TypeScript type `const d = 'up'`, `let d = 'up'` and `{ d: 'up' } as const`?
cards.back: `'up'` (literal), `string` (widened), and `{ readonly d: 'up' }`. A plain `const` object still has mutable `string` properties.

cards.front: In what order do you apply the rules that decide `this` at a call site?
cards.back: Arrow function (uses the enclosing scope's `this`) > `new` (fresh object) > bound function (the bound value) > `call`/`apply` (first argument) > `obj.m()` (the receiver) > plain call (`undefined` in strict code, `globalThis` in sloppy scripts).

cards.front: Why does `arr.forEach(obj.method)` throw when the method uses `this`, and how do you fix it?
cards.back: `obj.method` is just the function. `forEach` calls it plainly, so `this` is `undefined`. Fix it with `x => obj.method(x)`, `obj.method.bind(obj)`, `forEach(fn, obj)`, or an arrow class field.

cards.front: What four steps does `new F(...args)` perform?
cards.back: 1. Create a new object. 2. Set its `[[Prototype]]` to `F.prototype`. 3. Run `F` with `this` set to that object. 4. Return the object, unless the body returned an object or function, which replaces it. Returned primitives are ignored.

cards.front: With `a = Object.create(base)`, what is the difference between `a.x = 1` and `a.list.push(1)`?
cards.back: Assignment creates an own property on `a` that shadows `base.x`. `push` reads the inherited `base.list` and changes that one shared array, so every object linked to `base` sees the change.

cards.front: What does declaring `function f(this: Button)` give you in TypeScript?
cards.back: The fake first parameter is removed from the compiled output. TypeScript then checks every call site, so calling `f` without a `Button` as `this` is error TS2684. `OmitThisParameter<typeof f>` gives the type with `this` removed, which is what `bind` returns. Ordinary class methods don't declare `this`, so lint, not the compiler, catches extracted methods.

cards.front: List every falsy value in JavaScript.
cards.back: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including "0", [] and {}.

cards.front: When does `a ?? b` differ from `a || b`?
cards.back: When a is 0, "", false, NaN or 0n: `||` replaces any falsy value, `??` only null/undefined.

cards.front: How does `Object.is` differ from `===`?
cards.back: Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true and Object.is(0, -0) is false; otherwise identical.

cards.front: Outline how `x == y` converts operands.
cards.back: Same type → ===. null/undefined equal only each other. Boolean → number. number vs string → string to number. Object vs primitive → ToPrimitive. Then compare again.

cards.front: What does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` return and why?
cards.back: [1, 10, 9], sorted in place: with no comparator, elements are compared as strings by UTF-16 code units. Use (a, b) => a - b.

cards.front: In what order does the event loop serve synchronous code, microtasks and tasks?
cards.back: Run the current task (the script itself is one) to completion, then drain the entire microtask queue, including microtasks queued along the way, then take one task. Repeat. So: sync, then all microtasks, then `setTimeout(0)`.

cards.front: Which callbacks become microtasks and which become tasks?
cards.back: Microtasks: promise reactions (`then`/`catch`/`finally`), `await` continuations and `queueMicrotask`. Tasks: timers, I/O completions, UI events and messages.

cards.front: How much of an `async` function runs synchronously when you call it?
cards.back: Everything up to the first `await`. The rest resumes as a microtask, and the call returns a promise at once. A `new Promise` executor also runs synchronously.

cards.front: What is microtask starvation?
cards.back: Microtasks that keep queueing more microtasks never let the queue empty. Timers, I/O, input and painting then never run. Fix it by rescheduling each step with `setTimeout` so it becomes a separate task.

cards.front: Why doesn't `await Promise.resolve()` keep a long loop from blocking the page?
cards.back: It resumes as a microtask, which runs before any task or render step. To let other work run, yield to a task with `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0))`, or move heavy work to a worker.

cards.front: What does the next `.then` receive if a callback is `v => { work(v) }`?
cards.back: `undefined`. A block body with no `return` fulfils the next link right away, and the promise from `work` runs detached, so its errors escape the chain. Write `v => work(v)` or add `return`.

cards.front: When do `Promise.all`, `allSettled`, `race` and `any` settle?
cards.back: `all`: all fulfil (values in input order), or the first rejection. `allSettled`: once everything settles, and it never rejects. `race`: as soon as the first input settles, either way. `any`: the first fulfilment, or an `AggregateError` if every input rejects.

cards.front: Why is `xs.forEach(async x => { await work(x) })` a bug?
cards.back: `forEach` ignores the returned promises. Every item starts at once, the caller carries on before any of them finish, and rejections go unhandled. Use `for...of` with `await` to run in series, or `await Promise.all(xs.map(work))` to run in parallel.

cards.front: Inside `try/catch`, why write `return await p` instead of `return p`?
cards.back: `return p` leaves the `try` straight away, so a rejection skips the local `catch` and `finally` runs too early. `return await p` waits inside the `try`, so the `catch` handles the rejection.

cards.front: How do you run async jobs with at most k in flight and keep results in input order?
cards.back: Start `min(k, n)` lanes. Each lane is an async loop that claims `const i = next++`, awaits job `i` and stores the result in `results[i]`. Then `await Promise.all(lanes)`. `next++` is safe because JavaScript only switches between async functions at an `await`.

cards.front: What does `[10, 9, 1, 2].sort()` return, and why?
cards.back: `[1, 10, 2, 9]`. With no comparator, sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units. Use `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers.

cards.front: How do `sort` and `toSorted` differ?
cards.back: `sort` reorders the array in place and returns that same array. `toSorted` (ES2023) returns a new sorted array and leaves the original alone. It also exists on `ReadonlyArray`. The same pairing holds for reverse/toReversed and splice/toSpliced, plus `with` for index assignment.

cards.front: Name three ways a plain object differs from a Map as a key→value store.
cards.back: 1. Object keys are coerced to strings (so `1` and `'1'` collide); Map keeps any key type. 2. Objects inherit keys like `constructor` and treat `__proto__` specially; a Map has no inherited keys. 3. Objects list integer-like keys first in ascending order; Map iterates in insertion order and has an O(1) `size`.

cards.front: After `const c = { ...o }; c.tags.push('x')`, does `o.tags` change?
cards.back: Yes. Spread is shallow: `c.tags` points to the same array as `o.tags`. Use `structuredClone`, or copy the changed path: `{ ...o, tags: [...o.tags, 'x'] }`.

cards.front: Why replace `other.includes(x)` inside a `filter` with a Set?
cards.back: `includes` scans the array, so the filter is O(n·m). Build `new Set(other)` once (O(m)); then `has` is O(1) on average, for O(n + m) total. Sets compare objects by reference.

cards.front: Why does TypeScript accept a `Person` instance where a `Named` interface is expected, with no `implements`?
cards.back: Assignability is structural: any value with at least the required members (`name: string`) fits. Class names and declarations don't matter, and extra properties are allowed.

cards.front: When does TypeScript report an excess property error?
cards.back: Only when a fresh object literal goes straight into a typed slot (`const x: Named = { name, role }`). Put the same object in a variable first and it is accepted, because extra keys are only flagged on fresh literals.

cards.front: `interface B extends A` versus `type B = A & {...}` when a property type conflicts?
cards.back: `extends` gives a compile error at the declaration. The intersection gives no error: the property silently becomes `never`, and the failure shows up later wherever a value is created.

cards.front: `unknown` versus `any` for `JSON.parse` results?
cards.back: `any` turns checking off and spreads to everything it touches. `unknown` accepts any value but allows no use until you narrow it with `typeof`, `in`, `Array.isArray` or a type guard. Prefer `unknown` at boundaries.

cards.front: Does `JSON.parse(body) as User` validate the data?
cards.back: No. Types and `as` are erased when the compiler emits JavaScript, so nothing is checked at runtime. Parse to `unknown` and validate with guards or a schema library before trusting the value.

cards.front: How do you type a function that reads `obj[key]` so typos fail and the result has the property's type?
cards.back: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`. `K` is inferred as the literal key, the constraint rejects a key that isn't a property of `T`, and `T[K]` is that property's exact type.

cards.front: `const x: T = v` versus `const x = v satisfies T`: what's the difference?
cards.back: An annotation replaces the inferred type with `T`, so literal keys and values are lost. `satisfies` checks `v` against `T` but keeps the precise inferred type, so unknown keys such as `routes.hmoe` are compile errors. Use `satisfies` for config tables and lookup maps.

cards.front: Why does `Omit<User, 'pasword'>` compile, and does `Omit` remove the property at runtime?
cards.back: `Omit<T, K extends keyof any>` doesn't check `K` against `T`, so a typo removes nothing. A strict version is `type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>`. And no: utility types are erased, so the object keeps the property.

cards.front: When is a type parameter unnecessary?
cards.back: When it appears only once. `function show<T>(x: T): void` links nothing and is just `x: unknown`. A type parameter should relate at least two places, such as two parameters or a parameter and the return type. One that appears only in the return type, like `get<T>(): T`, is really an unchecked cast.

cards.front: How do you get the resolved value type of an async function `load` without restating it?
cards.back: `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>>`. `typeof` turns the value into a type, `ReturnType` gives `Promise<X>`, and `Awaited` unwraps it recursively. `Parameters<typeof load>` gives the argument tuple.

cards.front: Why model request state as a discriminated union instead of `{ loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: string }`?
cards.back: The bag of optionals admits nonsense such as loading with an error or success without data, and every read needs `?.` or `!`. A union with a literal tag (`status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'failure'`) lists only the legal states: illegal literals fail to compile, and checking the tag gives exactly that state's fields.

cards.front: How do you make a `switch` over a union fail to compile when a new variant is added?
cards.back: End it with `default: return assertNever(x)` where `function assertNever(x: never): never { throw ... }`. After all cases `x` is `never`; a new, unhandled variant leaves its type there, which is not assignable to `never`. At runtime the helper throws on data that does not match the types.

cards.front: Does TypeScript check that a type guard `x is T` or an assertion `asserts x is T` is correct?
cards.back: No. It only checks that the guard returns a boolean (or that the assertion returns nothing). The body is trusted, so `return 'name' in x` typed as `x is User` makes `{ name: 42 }` a `User`, and an empty assertion body asserts everything. Check every field and test guards with bad input.

cards.front: After `if (box.state.status === 'loading') { reset(); ... }`, is `box.state` still narrowed?
cards.back: Yes. Property narrowings are not invalidated by function calls, even if `reset` replaced `box.state`. The checker still says `loading`; at runtime it may be `idle`. Copy into a `const` before calling out, or re-check after the call.

cards.front: Does `strict: true` make `arr[0]` include `undefined`?
cards.back: No. `strict` turns on `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables` and others, but not `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. Without it, index 0 of an empty `number[]` is typed `number` and `.toFixed()` throws at runtime; with it, indexed reads are `T | undefined` and must be handled.

cards.front: What is `ToArray<string | number>` if `type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never`, and how do you stop that?
cards.back: `string[] | number[]`. A conditional type on a naked type parameter distributes: it runs once per union member and unions the results. Wrap both sides in a tuple, `[T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never`, to check the union as a whole and get `(string | number)[]`.

cards.front: How do you remove `readonly` and `?` with a mapped type?
cards.back: Prefix the modifier with `-`: `{ -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` is a `Mutable<T>` and `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` is `Required<T>` (it also strips the `undefined` the `?` added). Mapping over `keyof T` is homomorphic, so it keeps existing modifiers and maps arrays and tuples to arrays and tuples.

cards.front: How do you rename or drop keys in a mapped type?
cards.back: Use an `as` clause (TS 4.1+): `{ [K in keyof T as NewKey]: T[K] }`. A template literal such as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}` renames keys; remapping to `never` removes the key, e.g. `as K extends 'password' ? never : K`. The value type still uses the original `K`.

cards.front: How is `ReturnType` written, and what does `infer` do?
cards.back: `type ReturnType<F extends (...args: any) => any> = F extends (...args: any) => infer R ? R : any`. `infer R` declares a type variable filled in by matching the pattern; it is only allowed in a conditional type's `extends` clause. On an overloaded function it matches the last signature.

cards.front: What goes wrong with a naive recursive `DeepReadonly<T>`?
cards.back: Mapping over a function drops its call signature, so return functions unchanged first. `Map`, `Set` and `Date` are mapped member by member and keep mutating methods. Deep or infinite instantiation fails with TS2589. And it is compile-time only: you still need a recursive `Object.freeze` to stop writes at runtime.

cards.front: A module does `count++` after exporting `count`. Who sees the new value: an ESM `import { count }` or a CJS `const { count } = require(...)`?
cards.back: Only the ESM import. ESM imports are live, read-only bindings to the exporter's variable. CJS `module.exports = { count }` copies the value at that moment, and destructuring copies it again. Objects are shared either way; only the binding differs. Note that `export default count` is a one-time value too.

cards.front: What does a circular import see in CommonJS and in ES modules?
cards.back: CJS: the second `require` returns the half-built `module.exports`, so properties assigned later read as `undefined`, and a later `module.exports = {...}` replacement is never seen. ESM: bindings are linked, but a `let`/`const`/`class` export read before its declaration runs throws a TDZ `ReferenceError`. Hoisted function declarations work. Fix: move shared code to a third module or read lazily.

cards.front: Why is `e` typed `unknown` in `catch (e)`, and how do you use it?
cards.back: Anything can be thrown, so strict mode (`useUnknownInCatchVariables`) types it `unknown`, and only `unknown` or `any` annotations are allowed. Narrow with `instanceof Error` (or a subclass), normalise other values with a `toError` that wraps them and sets `cause`, and rethrow what you cannot handle.

cards.front: What happens if a `finally` block contains `return`?
cards.back: It replaces the pending completion: an earlier `return` is overridden and an exception in flight is silently discarded. Use `finally` only for cleanup. Also, `return x` computes `x` before `finally` runs, so reassigning `x` in `finally` does not change the returned value.

cards.front: When should a function return a `Result` union instead of throwing?
cards.back: Return `{ ok: true; value } | { ok: false; error }` for expected failures the caller must handle (validation, parse errors, not found, declined payment): the type forces the `ok` check. Throw for bugs, broken invariants and failures only a top-level handler can deal with. Convert at the boundary and keep one style per layer.

cards.front: In `class Child extends Base`, when do Child's field initialisers run, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Right after `super()` returns: base fields, base constructor body, then derived fields, then the derived constructor body. If the base constructor calls a method Child overrides, that override sees Child's fields as `undefined`. Don't call overridable methods from constructors.

cards.front: `private secret` versus `#secret`: what is different at runtime?
cards.back: `private` is erased: `secret` is a normal enumerable property, visible to `Object.keys`/`JSON.stringify` and reachable via `obj['secret']`. `#secret` is a JavaScript private slot: unreachable outside the class body (even by subclasses), not listed anywhere, and `#secret in obj` is a brand check.

cards.front: Is `const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 }` allowed for `class Point { constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {} }`? Is `p instanceof Point`?
cards.back: Allowed: class instance types are structural. But `p instanceof Point` is false because it was never constructed by `Point`. Adding a `private`, `protected` or `#` member makes the class nominal and rejects look-alikes.

cards.front: What goes wrong with `memoize` keyed by `String(args)`, and what is a better default?
cards.back: Keys collide: `[1]` and `['1']` both give `'1'`, and every object becomes `'[object Object]'`. Use `JSON.stringify(args)` (or a caller-supplied `keyOf`), a `WeakMap` for identity keys, check `cache.has(key)` so `undefined` results stay cached, and bound the cache.

cards.front: Does `Object.freeze` or `as const` make data immutable?
cards.back: `Object.freeze` is enforced at runtime but shallow: nested arrays/objects stay writable. `as const` (like `readonly`) is compile-time only. Prefer returning new values: spread, `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `with` (ES2023).

cards.front: What is the difference between a stub, a fake, a spy and a mock?
cards.back: A stub returns canned answers and checks nothing. A fake is a working but simpler implementation, such as an in-memory store. A spy records calls so you can assert on them afterwards. A mock is set up with expectations and fails if they are not met. Prefer injecting fakes through parameters over module mocking.

cards.front: How do you make code that uses `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` testable?
cards.back: Make them parameters. Pass a `Clock` with `now()` (production wraps `Date.now`, tests use a `FakeClock` with `advance(ms)`) and an `Rng` (`() => number`; production passes `Math.random`, tests pass a seeded generator). A default parameter keeps existing call sites unchanged.

cards.front: Why not `await sleep(100)` in a test, and what do you do instead?
cards.back: A sleep guesses how long the work takes: too short and the test flakes, too long and the suite is slow. Await the promise the code returns, or use fake timers (`vi.useFakeTimers()`, `advanceTimersByTime`) to move time by hand. Always return or await an async test's promise.

cards.front: The code type-checks. Why does it still need tests?
cards.back: Types are erased at run time and check shapes, not values. A function typed `number` can still return `NaN`, an off-by-one index or `-1`, and JSON from the network is whatever the server sent. Types remove a class of bugs, while tests check behaviour and boundaries.

cards.front: Name the main differences between Node and the browser as JavaScript hosts.
cards.back: Globals: `window`/`document` versus `process`/`Buffer`, with `globalThis` in both. I/O: DOM and storage versus `node:fs`/`net`, while `fetch`, `URL` and timers exist in both. Event loop: Node adds `process.nextTick` and `setImmediate`, and browsers add rendering steps. Threads: Web Workers versus `worker_threads`. Trust: a same-origin sandbox versus full OS access.

cards.front: What is wrong with `new Array(3).fill(new Array(3).fill(0))` for a grid, and what do you write instead?
cards.back: `fill` evaluates its argument once, so all three slots hold the same row array and writing `grid[0][0]` changes every row. Use `Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(0))` so the factory makes one array per row.

cards.front: Why does `['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)` return `[1, NaN, NaN]`?
cards.back: `map` calls its callback with (value, index, array), so the index becomes `parseInt`'s radix: radix 0 means base 10, radix 1 is invalid, and '3' is not a binary digit. Use `map(Number)` or `map(s => parseInt(s, 10))`.

cards.front: Why avoid `queue.shift()` in BFS, and what is the idiom instead?
cards.back: `shift` removes index 0 and moves every other element down, O(n) per call, so BFS can become O(n²). Keep pushing to the end and read with a head index: `for (let head = 0; head < queue.length; head++) { const node = queue[head]; ... }`.

cards.front: In an array-backed binary heap, what are the parent and child indexes of `i`, and what do push and pop do?
cards.back: Parent `(i - 1) >> 1`, children `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`. push appends and sifts up while the item beats its parent; pop takes the root, moves the last item to index 0 and sifts down to the better child. Both O(log n). JavaScript has no built-in heap.

cards.front: A comparator does `(a.time ?? Infinity) - (b.time ?? Infinity)`. What breaks?
cards.back: When both times are missing, `Infinity - Infinity` is `NaN`, which the sort treats as 0, so those items keep whatever order they arrived in and no tie-break applies. Return a number from separate comparators chained with explicit tie-breaks, and return 0 for the time key when either side is `null`.
